You use the gerund, the present participle and the verbal adjective to express simultaneity, manner and cause, and to write in the style of job ads and professional letters.
By becoming director, you would keep your name on the door.
Having founded this firm alone, I want to choose who will take it over.
Form the present participle (the “nous” stem + -ant) and the irregular forms ayant, étant, sachant.
Use the gerund (en + -ant) for simultaneity, manner, means and condition.
Use “tout en + -ant” for simultaneity with a nuance of contrast.
Use the present participle in writing, instead of a relative clause or a cause.
Tell the present participle (invariable) apart from the verbal adjective (which agrees and is sometimes spelt differently).
Monday, 13 September 2032. Nathalie Fabre, who founded the architecture firm in 1998, is waiting for Ioana, her partner, in the meeting room with the door closed. She has important news.
Sit down, Ioana. What I have to tell you isn’t easy. Thinking about it all summer, I’ve made a decision.
You’re worrying me. You’re not ill, at least?
No, don’t worry. But I’m sixty-three. Having founded this firm alone, I want to choose myself the person who will take it over.
At the end of next year. And I’d like it to be you. By becoming director, you’d keep your name on the door, but you’d also have everything else.
Everything else? You mean the bank?
The bank, the employees, the demanding clients. It’s tiring work, I won’t lie to you. But you learn by doing it.
Then I’ll sell to a big group. Since the employees would risk losing their jobs, I’d rather avoid that.
You know I love drawing. Running the firm, I won’t have time any more.
You’ll draw less, that’s true. But you’ll decide what we draw. That’s quite convincing, isn’t it?
(smiling) While being very convincing, you’re forgetting one thing: I’ll have to buy out your share.
I’m not forgetting anything. We’ll talk about it while walking, tomorrow at noon. I’ve already booked a table.
It is formed from the stem of the “nous” form of the present + -ant. It is invariable. Three verbs are irregular:
The compound form (ayant / étant + past participle) shows an earlier action: “Ayant fondé ce cabinet seule…” = Having founded this firm alone…
The gerund (en + present participle) describes an action done by the SAME subject as the main verb. It can express:
En devenant directrice, tu garderais ton nom.
If you became director, you would keep your name.

The subject of the gerund must be the same as that of the main verb! “En arrivant au bureau, le téléphone a sonné.” ✗ (the phone doesn’t arrive at the office). Correct: “En arrivant au bureau, j’ai entendu le téléphone.”
“Tout” strengthens the gerund. It shows either two strictly simultaneous actions or a contrast (= although):
She works while listening to music at the same time.
Although you’re very convincing, you’re forgetting one thing.
While staying in Lyon, she will also build in Romania.
Romanian has a single gerund (“-ând”) for both French constructions. When translating “en + -ant” with a different subject or a cause, consider whether it is actually a present participle.
Without “en”, the present participle belongs to written register (ads, reports, letters). It replaces a relative clause with “qui” or expresses a cause:
Firm seeking an architect who speaks Romanian. (= qui recherche, qui parle)
Since the employees risk losing their jobs, I’d rather avoid that. (cause)
Having been born in Iași, she speaks Romanian.
Unlike the gerund, the present participle can refer to a different subject from that of the main verb: “Les salariés risquant…, je préférerais…” is correct.
The verbal adjective describes a quality, AGREES and is sometimes spelt differently. The present participle describes an action and is invariable:
différant (des avis différant sur ce point)
Tip: if you can put “très” in front, it’s a verbal adjective: “un travail très fatigant”. If it has an object or “en”, it’s a participle: “en fatiguant tout le monde”.

En arrivant au bureau, j’ai entendu le téléphone.

The start of the school year in September 2032 was the busiest the family had ever known. Rose-Hélène moved up to the middle section, in Mrs Chevalier’s class, who had asked to keep her one more year. Henri-Ion started nursery, crying on the first day, smiling on the second and refusing to come home on the third. And Inès started at the lycée, her clarinet on her back.

Julien, for his part, left almost every week. The eight new halls were progressing at the same time, in eight different places in France, and he spent his life on trains, reading quotes, answering emails, sometimes sleeping with his head against the window. He came home on Friday evening, exhausted, and left again on Monday morning, taking a box of frozen sarmale that Lucia made for him.

Ioana had her own building site. For three years she had been Nathalie Fabre’s partner, and the copper plaque at the entrance of the building on rue de la République bore both names: “Fabre & Popescu, architects”. The firm employed fourteen people. That year it had signed the biggest contract in its history: converting an old hospital into social housing in the Guillotière district.

On Monday 13 September, arriving at the office, Ioana found Nathalie already settled in the meeting room, a cup of coffee in her hand, the door closed. It was unusual. Nathalie always arrived last, running, apologising, looking for her glasses. That morning she had been there since seven. She looked serious. She motioned to Ioana to come in and close the door behind her.

“I’m sixty-three,” Nathalie began. “I founded this firm in 1998, working alone in an attic room, with a second-hand drawing board. I made it grow by fighting for every client, every competition, every building permit. And I’ve decided to stop at the end of next year.” Ioana said nothing. She had half expected it. She wasn’t ready all the same.

“I’d like you to be the one who takes over the firm,” Nathalie went on. “Not just as a partner. As director. With everything that involves: the fourteen employees, the clients, the bank, the taxes, the sleepless nights. I know you love drawing. I loved drawing too. But a firm isn’t just drawings. It’s a business. And a business has to be run.”

Ioana asked how long she had to think it over. Nathalie answered: until Christmas. Then they would need a year to organise the transition, introduce Ioana to the clients, and negotiate with the bank the buyout of Nathalie’s shares. For there was a financial detail, which Nathalie explained with a half-smile: to take over the firm, Ioana would have to buy her share. And her share was worth a lot of money.

Leaving the meeting room, Ioana walked through the open-plan office looking at each employee as if she were seeing them for the first time. Sophie, the accountant, who knew every figure by heart. Karim, the draughtsman, who listened to jazz while working. Hugo, the youngest architect, brilliant and impatient, who threatened to resign every six months. Fourteen people. Fourteen families. And soon, perhaps, fourteen salaries to pay every month, while sleeping badly.

That evening, Ioana told Julien all this on the phone. He was in Brest, in an old fish market that would become a music hall, and you could hear the gulls behind him. He listened without interrupting. Then he asked her what she wanted. Not what was reasonable. Not what Nathalie expected. What she wanted. Ioana replied that she didn’t know. It was the truth.

Two days later, on Wednesday 15 September, her phone rang while she was having lunch. A Romanian number. A man’s voice, very polite, speaking the impeccable Romanian of a headhunter. His name was Mihai Dobre. He worked for Arhimar, the biggest architecture firm in Bucharest. Arhimar was opening a new department devoted to renovating old buildings, and was looking for someone to run it.

“Someone with European experience,” Mihai Dobre specified. “Someone who speaks Romanian, French and English. Someone who knows the European Union’s renovation standards. And, if possible, someone born in Iași, because our managing director is from Iași and is very attached to his home town.” He laughed. Ioana didn’t laugh. She asked how he had got her name.

From an article, he replied. An article published in Romania in the spring, after the “Odile’s Silence” video, telling the family’s story. It mentioned Radu, the engineer building music halls all over France. And it mentioned his sister, Ioana Popescu, “partner in a renowned Lyon architecture firm”. Arhimar’s managing director had read the article over his coffee. He had asked for her to be found.

The salary offered was double what she earned in Lyon. There would be a company flat in the centre of Bucharest, a car, a place at the French school for the children. And above all, there would be the chance to do in Romania what she did in France: save old buildings instead of demolishing them. Mihai Dobre suggested she come and visit the offices in October, all expenses paid.

Ioana hung up, trembling. She stayed sitting on the café terrace, her salad untouched in front of her, watching the trams go by on rue de la République. In less than a week, she had been offered two lives. One here, at the head of Nathalie’s firm, with debts and responsibilities. The other over there, in the country she had left six years earlier, with a double salary and a company car.

She didn’t talk about it to anyone for three days. Not even to Julien, who was still in Brest. She went to the office, drew, answered clients, picked up the children, pretending everything was normal. But Rose-Hélène, who was four and a half and noticed everything, asked her on Friday evening why she had eyes “that think too much”.

Julien came home that evening, late, bringing Breton crêpes bought at Brest station. Ioana waited for him on the balcony. She told him everything at once, speaking very fast, mixing French and Romanian. Julien listened to the end. Then he asked just one question: “And your mother? Does she know?” Ioana shook her head. That was exactly what frightened her.

Because Ioana knew her mother. If Elena found out her daughter had been offered a job in Bucharest, four hundred kilometres from Iași instead of two thousand, she would talk about nothing else, day and night, for months. She would make lists. She would call cousins. She would find flats. And Ioana would no longer be able to think calmly. So she had to decide alone first. Talk about it afterwards.

Julien suggested a method he had learnt while running the network. Take a big sheet of paper. Draw two columns. Write down everything you would gain and everything you would lose, in each case. Not just money. Everything. They spent the night on the balcony, drinking tea, eating cold crêpes, filling in the sheet. At three in the morning there were forty lines. It didn’t get them much further.

In the “Bucharest” column there was the salary, family closer by, Grandma getting older, the pleasure of building in her own language, the pride of coming home a success. In the “Lyon” column there was the firm, Nathalie, the orchestra, Odile, the lime tree, Rose-Hélène’s school, Julien’s work, and a line Ioana had written last, in small letters, without explanation: “the landing”.

She decided to go to Bucharest. Not to accept. To see. She didn’t want to turn down an offer without having looked it in the face. Julien agreed. He would look after the children. On Saturday 9 October, Ioana flew from Lyon to Bucharest, with a grey suit in her suitcase and a file of projects under her arm. On the plane, flying over the Alps, she thought of her grandmother, forehead pressed to the window.

Bucharest surprised her. She hadn’t been back since a student internship, years earlier. The city had changed spectacularly. There were glass towers, trendy cafés, scooters everywhere, young people speaking English on the metro. But there were also, on street corners, those old nineteenth-century houses, with their wrought-iron balconies and crumbling façades, waiting for someone to save them.

Arhimar’s offices occupied the top three floors of a new tower, with a view over the whole city. The managing director, Mr Ciobanu, a man of about fifty, smiling and energetic, received her himself. He showed her round the studios, talking non-stop, pointing at models, quoting impressive figures. Two hundred employees. Projects in six countries. Turnover growing by thirty percent a year.

Then he took her to lunch at an elegant restaurant near the Romanian Athenaeum. He talked to her about Iași, about his childhood in the Țicău district, about the street where he had grown up. He even knew the lycée where Ioana had studied. He was charming, cultured, convincing. And over dessert, he made her his official offer, in writing, in a cream envelope with Arhimar’s gold logo.

Ioana opened the envelope trying to keep a calm face. The figures were even better than on the phone. There was a relocation bonus. Profit-sharing. And a sentence at the end, handwritten by Mr Ciobanu himself: “Come home. Romania needs people like you.” Ioana put the letter back in the envelope. She said she would reply before Christmas.

In the afternoon she had free time. She could have rested at the hotel. She preferred to walk. She walked for four hours, without a plan, following the streets at random, looking at the façades. In a little street behind Piața Romană, she stopped in front of an abandoned house, very beautiful, with a wrought-iron balcony shaped like waves and a carved wooden door, half rotten.

An old lady was sitting on a bench just opposite, feeding the pigeons. She saw Ioana looking at the house. She asked her, in Romanian, whether she was an architect. Ioana said yes. The old lady nodded. She said she had been born in that house in 1940, and had been waiting for thirty years for someone to come and repair it. Then she asked: “Are you going to repair it?”

Ioana didn’t know what to answer. She sat down on the bench next to the old lady, and they talked for an hour. About the house, the city, the war, communism, the children gone abroad. The old lady had three grandchildren: one in London, one in Madrid, one in Toronto. She only saw them once a year. “All the young people leave,” she said without sadness. “It’s normal. But the houses stay.”

That evening, in her hotel room on the twentieth floor, Ioana video-called Julien. The children were already in their pyjamas. Rose-Hélène wanted to see Bucharest. Ioana turned the phone towards the window, towards the city lights. Rose-Hélène looked for a long time. Then she asked where Fourvière was. Ioana explained that there was no Fourvière in Bucharest. Rose-Hélène found that very sad.

That evening she had dinner with Andreea, a former fellow student who now worked for a bank in one of the glass towers. Andreea had two children, a big flat and a husband she hardly ever saw. She listened to the Arhimar story while eating a salad. Then she said: “You know, Ioana, you speak Romanian with a French accent now.” Ioana laughed. She had never noticed.

“If you come back,” Andreea went on, “you’ll earn a lot of money. You’ll work twelve hours a day. You’ll see your children on Sundays. Like me.” She said it smiling, without bitterness, the way you note that it’s raining. Then she asked to see photos of Lyon. Ioana showed her the balcony, Fourvière, the La Duchère lime tree, Rose-Hélène with her harmonica. Andreea looked for a long time. She added nothing.

On Sunday, Ioana took the train to Iași. She couldn’t come to Romania without seeing her mother and grandmother, even for a single day. But she said nothing about the offer. She said she had come for an architects’ conference. Elena believed her. Grandma, on the other hand, looked at her for a long time over her glasses while peeling potatoes, and said nothing. Grandma never said anything when she knew.

In Iași nothing had changed, and that was exactly what was so moving. The same grey block, the same stairwell smelling of cabbage, the same rug in the hall. Dan showed her the little garden he grew behind the block, showing her each tomato like a treasure. Elena had cooked enough food for twenty people, apologising for not having had time to make more.

That evening, while Elena was doing the washing-up, Grandma took Ioana aside, into the little bedroom where Ioana had slept all her childhood. She closed the door. Then she said, very calmly: “They’ve asked you to come back.” It wasn’t a question. Ioana nodded. Grandma asked whether it paid well. Ioana told her the figure. Grandma whistled through her teeth. She had been whistling more and more since the summer.

“Listen to me carefully,” said Grandma. “I’m eighty-six. I’ve seen all the young people leave this country. Your mother, your brother, you. And I’ll tell you something nobody else will. Don’t come back for me. Don’t come back for your mother. Don’t come back for the money. Only come back if your home is here.” She laid her wrinkled hand on Ioana’s heart. “And your home, I think you know where it is.”

Ioana cried in the little bedroom, on her grandmother’s shoulder, as when she was seven. Grandma let her cry, stroking her hair. Then she gave her an embroidered handkerchief, told her to blow her nose, and announced she had made plăcinte for her to take back to the children. There were three kilos. Grandma had never understood the concept of baggage allowance.

On the flight home on Monday, Ioana thought it all over again. Mr Ciobanu and his cream envelope. The old lady on the bench and her house with the wave-shaped balcony. Her grandmother and her wrinkled hand. And flying over the Alps, at the very moment her grandmother had heard someone whistling, she understood that she had already made her decision. She had probably made it long ago, without knowing.

But a new idea had been born during the trip. An idea she had had on the bench, listening to the old lady. Why choose between Lyon and Bucharest? Why not do both, differently? The Fabre & Popescu firm knew how to renovate old buildings. Arhimar had clients, money and houses to save. They could work together. Staying in Lyon. While building in Romania.

On Tuesday morning, arriving at the office, Ioana went straight to Nathalie’s office. She closed the door. Nathalie looked up from her plans, worried. Ioana told her everything: the phone call, Bucharest, the glass tower, the cream envelope, the old lady, Grandma. Nathalie listened without interrupting, turning her pencil between her fingers. At the end she asked simply: “Well?”

“Well, I accept,” said Ioana. “I’ll take over the firm. But on one condition. I want to start a collaboration with Arhimar. Not an office over there. A collaboration. Joint projects, architect exchanges, renovation sites in Romania supervised from Lyon. I don’t want to choose between my two countries. I want to build a bridge.” Nathalie put down her pencil. She looked at Ioana for a long time.

Then she opened her desk drawer and took out an old iron key, all rusty, tied to a red ribbon. “It’s the key to my attic room,” she said. “The one where I founded the firm in 1998. I’ve kept it for twenty-four years. I wanted to give it to the person who would replace me.” She put the key in Ioana’s hand. “A bridge,” she repeated, smiling. “You see, that’s exactly why I chose you.”

Mr Ciobanu still had to be convinced. Ioana called him on Thursday, carefully preparing each sentence, writing her arguments on a card as Inès had taught her. She began by turning down the job. There was a long silence on the line. Then she made her proposal. A collaboration between equals. Lyon know-how, Romanian clients. And a first joint project, a symbolic one: an abandoned house behind Piața Romană.

Mr Ciobanu laughed. A big, sincere laugh, very different from his business-lunch laugh. He said that in twenty-five years of career, nobody had ever turned down a job by offering him something better in exchange. He asked for a week to think. He called back after two days. He accepted. And he wanted to know who owned the house behind Piața Romană.

That left the question of money. The following Monday, Ioana and Nathalie went together to the bank on rue de la Bourse to meet Mr Perrin, the adviser who had looked after the firm for fifteen years. He was a cautious man with thick glasses, who spoke slowly, weighing every word. He studied the firm’s accounts for an hour, turning the pages one by one, noting figures in the margin.

Then he looked up. “The firm is sound,” he said. “Turnover is stable, the clients are loyal, and the Guillotière contract is reassuring. I can grant you a ten-year loan to buy out Mrs Fabre’s shares.” He added, looking at Ioana over his glasses: “But by signing, madam, you are committing yourself for ten years. No going off to Bucharest.” Ioana smiled. News travelled fast in Lyon.

That left the hardest part: Elena. Ioana chose to announce everything at once, on a Sunday, by video, with Julien beside her and the children on her knees. Turning down Bucharest. Taking over the firm. The collaboration. Elena listened in silence, which almost never happened. Then she said she had always known her daughter wouldn’t come back. Then she cried. Then she asked when Ioana would come to Bucharest for the first site.

Ioana answered: in the spring. Elena said she would take the train from Iași to come and watch her work. Then she added, lowering her voice, that she already had a list of cousins in Bucharest who could put her up. Ioana laughed. So did Julien. And behind Elena, on the screen, Grandma walked past in her apron and gave Ioana a little wink before disappearing into the kitchen.

The following Friday, at the firm, Nathalie gathered the fourteen employees in the big room. She announced her retirement at the end of the following year, and Ioana’s appointment as director. There was a silence. Then Hugo, the youngest architect, the one who threatened to resign every six months, was the first to stand up. He said: “At last someone who understands our hours.” Everyone applauded.

The next week, Ioana had her first real test as director. Hugo came to see her, looking gloomy, a letter in his hand. A Paris agency was offering him a better-paid job. He was hesitating. Ioana didn’t make a speech. She asked him what he was missing here. Hugo answered, after a long silence: time. He wanted to be able to work from home on Fridays, to look after his daughter.

Ioana thought it over, looking out of the window. Then she said yes. On condition that he train the firm’s two interns in return. Hugo agreed, smiling for the first time in weeks. Leaving the office, he tore up the Paris agency’s letter and threw it in the bin. Nathalie, who had seen everything through the glass, gave a thumbs-up. Ioana had just learnt her job by doing it.

That evening, Ioana walked home, crossing the Rhône by the footbridge, watching the barges, the lights, the hill of Fourvière shining. In her pocket she held Nathalie’s old rusty key. She was thinking of the house behind Piața Romană, of the old lady feeding the pigeons, of the bridge she was going to build, and she felt, for the first time in a long while, exactly where she belonged.

Arriving at rue d’Austerlitz, she found the flat door open, as always. On the other side of the landing, Isabelle’s door was open too. Rose-Hélène was running from one to the other in her pyjamas, with her harmonica. Henri-Ion was toddling after her. Isabelle, on the doorstep, was pretending to scold them, laughing. And Julien, in the kitchen, was warming up the last of Grandma’s plăcinte.

Ioana stopped in the middle of the landing, between the two open doors. She took Nathalie’s old key out of her pocket and looked at it for a moment under the yellow light of the stairwell. Then she put it back in her pocket. She didn’t need a key here. Here, the doors stayed open. Rose-Hélène stopped in front of her, looked up and asked: “Do you still have your eyes that think too much?”

Ioana laughed. She took her daughter in her arms, very tightly. “No,” she answered. “Not any more.” Rose-Hélène looked satisfied. She played the three notes to celebrate. Ioana whistled the next three, for the first time since Bucharest. And in the kitchen, Julien, without turning round, whistled the rest, stirring the pan, with the quiet smile of someone who had always known how the story would end.

Offre d’emploi : directeur ou directrice du département Rénovation
Arhimar, an architecture firm with more than two hundred staff and active in six European countries, is looking for a director for its new department devoted to heritage renovation.

Profile: qualified architect with at least ten years’ experience, including five in a European Union country. You master European energy-renovation standards. Speaking Romanian, English and French fluently, you know how to lead an international team.
Duties: working directly with senior management, you will define the department’s strategy. You will steer renovation projects while developing new partnerships.
We offer: an attractive salary, profit-sharing, company accommodation in central Bucharest and a place at an international school for your children. As travel is frequent, a company car is provided.

Position available from January 2033. Applications, including a CV and a cover letter, must be sent before 31 October. Candidates who have not received a reply within a month may consider that their application has not been successful.
